content: FAN1, also known as FANCD2/FANCI-associated nuclease 1 (KIAA1018), is an enzyme encoded by the FAN1 gene in humans. It functions as a structure-dependent endonuclease and belongs to the myotubularin-related class 1 cysteine-based protein tyrosine phosphatases. FAN1 is believed to play a critical role in the Fanconi Anemia (FA) DNA repair pathway. Structure FAN1 is a protein composed of 1017 amino acids. The crystal structures of its residues 373-1017 have been characterized, revealing three distinct domains: the SAP domain (the primary DNA-binding domain), the TPR domain (responsible for interdomain interactions and dimerization), and the VRR_NUC module (the catalytic site). DNA binding promotes the dimerization of FAN1 in a head-to-tail configuration. The SAP domain contains three major components: α9, α5β1, and α7. The α9 helix stabilizes the protein during dimerization and mediates interactions between α5β1 and α7 as they adjust their positions. These configurations correspond to substrate scanning, substrate latching, and substrate unwinding. In the FAN1 dimer, the SAP domains of both enzymes interact with the DNA duplex (dsDNA), facilitating DNA-induced dimerization and guiding single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) into the SAP domain of the downstream enzyme (PSAP). The SAP domain of the upstream enzyme (ASAP) assists in directing DNA to PSAP. The SAP surface facing the catalytic site is the most conserved region among FAN1 homologs and is positively charged to enable favorable hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions with DNA. Specific residues, such as Y374 and Y436, form hydrogen bonds with the DNA phosphate backbone. FAN1 can bind DNA in either orientation, but substrate latching and unwinding cannot occur when the 5' flap is oriented away from the VRR_NUC site. The unresolved portion of FAN1 contains a zinc finger at the N-terminus, known as the UBZ region, which is conserved across eukaryotes and is present in proteins that bind ubiquitinated proteins. This zinc finger is essential for recruitment to the ubiquitinated FANCD2/FANCI complex and is also found in other nucleases. The VRR_NUC catalytic domain, located at the C-terminus, provides endonuclease functionality. FAN1 represents the first known instance of a virus-type replication-repair nuclease module in eukaryotes, which is typically found as a standalone domain in bacterial and viral Holliday Junction Resolvases (HJRs). However, FAN1 does not exhibit activity on Holliday Junction substrates, likely due to a subdomain of SAP (comprising six α helices) that inhibits HJR activity. Function Interstrand DNA crosslinks (ICLs) obstruct the progression of transcription and replication machinery. The resolution of these blocks, known as unhooking, requires incisions on one strand of the DNA duplex on either side of the ICL. Repair of ICLs is triggered when the DNA replication fork stalls, and the FA proteins, in conjunction with FAN1, play a critical role in removing these lesions. The FA pathway involves 15 known proteins, three of which form the FA AP24-MHF1/2 complex that recognizes ICLs at stalled replication forks. This complex recruits the FA core complex, consisting of eight proteins, which monoubiquitinates FANCD2 and FANCI, enabling them to form a heterodimer. This heterodimer recruits FAN1 and other nucleases, such as SLX4. Ubiquitinated FANCD2 interacts with FAN1, which, upon recruitment, restrains DNA replication fork progression and prevents chromosomal abnormalities during fork stalling. FAN1 is typically localized in the nucleus but forms distinct foci at damaged regions in the presence of ICLs. The protein exhibits both endonuclease and exonuclease activities to remove ICLs. At a replication fork arrested by an ICL, FAN1 catalyzes incisions in the double-stranded region, unhooking the crosslink and separating the DNA strands through two incision events. This process yields one strand with a crosslinked nucleotide and another strand with a gap. FAN1 preferentially acts as a 5' flap endonuclease, cleaving approximately five nucleotides from a junction. It can also incise at splayed arms, three-way junctions, and 3' flaps, though with decreasing preference. At high concentrations, FAN1 exhibits 3' to 5' exonuclease activity. On blunt-end substrates, FAN1 also processes 5' recessed ends. However, FAN1 does not bind single-stranded DNA. The presence of the FANCD2/FANCI complex is unaffected by FAN1 knockdown, as FAN1 acts downstream of FANCD2/FANCI recruitment. FAN1 has also been shown to increase the frequency of homologous recombination (HR), suggesting that the gapped intermediate formed after ICL unhooking may be repaired through HR when homologous chromosomes are available. FAN1 does not appear to participate in other types of DNA repair, as it does not localize to DNA following irradiation. Clinical Significance Mutations in any of the 15 known FA genes are associated with Fanconi anemia, a recessive autosomal disorder characterized by congenital abnormalities, anemia, bone marrow failure, and cancer predisposition in childhood. However, some patients exhibit unassigned Fanconi anemia, where no mutations in the known FA genes are identified. Mutations in FAN1 can lead to chronic kidney diseases and neurological conditions such as schizophrenia. Recent research has questioned the classification of FAN1 as an FA gene. Analysis of blood samples from FAN1-deficient individuals revealed only mild sensitivity to ICL agents and chromosomal fragility consistent with Fanconi anemia. FAN1 deficiency increases in vitro sensitivity to cisplatin and mitomycin C, two crosslinking agents. FAN1 is also capable of repairing mitomycin C-induced double-strand breaks. Germline mutations in the FAN1 gene can cause hereditary colorectal cancer due to defective DNA repair.
